text:
I stopped by FedNuts at around 3pm yesterday for a quick late lunch after getting into Philly on the train.  I wasn't planning to stop by, per se, but since I didn't have any cash on me, I couldn't hit the food cart I wanted to try.  I decided to try FedNuts instead since it was located between the train station and the location of my meeting and I have a soft spot for fried chicken and donuts.

Given that most of the chicken comes by the half or whole bird, I decided to go with the chicken sandwich ($6.75), which consisted of a chicken breast, spicy sauce, and pickles, reminiscent of a Chick-Fil-A sandwich.  It was a bit greasy, but was quite delicious, easily beating its fast food cousin.  The chicken was crisp on the outside and moist on the inside, as good fried chicken should be.  The spicy sauce added a nice kick, and the tartness of the pickles cut the richness of the rest of the sandwich nicely.

Since all of the fancy donuts were out at the time of my visit, I also ordered a strawberry lavender hot and fresh donut ($2.50).  True to its name, the donut was served hot out of the fryer, and the smell was quite intoxicating, so I didn't delay to nosh on it immediately while waiting for my sandwich and while walking to my destination.  The donut was a bit different than what I expected--rather than being glazed, it's coated with a sugary mixture incorporating strawberries and lavender seed.  While I enjoyed it, I'm not sure that it's worth 2.5 times the price of a donut at Beiler's, which has the best donuts I've ever put in my mouth, bar none.

Overall, I enjoyed my tasty and reasonably-priced (albeit unhealthy...) lunch from FedNuts.  Though there were only two employees working at the time of my visit, they were friendly and efficient--my order came out in about 5 min.  Though I'd return to try the chicken (which I understand comes with different rubs, etc., for regular orders), I'll stick to Beiler's to satisfy my donut cravings when in Philly.
llama_8b_pred_reasoning: The review is overwhelmingly positive, with the reviewer enjoying the food and service. All models agree on a high rating, with BERT being the most confident, indicating a strong sentiment towards FedNuts.

Honestly, I've tried so hard to love Noble Pie. The atmosphere is relaxed, the decor is unique, and the location is convenient and historical. The food is generally pretty quality when done right, and the names are creative in that independent-and-quirky-restaurant sort of way.

There is a clear view into the kitchen in the back, where it's almost painfully easy to see the ever-changing cook crew lounging about, fucking around, or being a little too friendly with the food (not the most sanitary bunch). 

The wait is long. I'm a patient person. I have no problem waiting for my food when it's quality stuff. If you're willing to brave a wait, it might be worth it to you, but I'm just saying: be warned. An order of wings and a pizza will set you back about thirty to forty minutes. It's not excessive, but it is a while to wait in a restaurant.

Now for my own experience. Nobly Pie advertises themselves as vegan friendly, which lends a great opportunity to Renoites and visitors who have alternative food tastes or food allergies. I happen to be one of those people. Unfortunately, on no less than three occasions, I have placed very specific orders for totally vegan pizzas (which are NOT cheap even regularly, mind you), only to be disappointed by genuine non-vegan cheeses, milk-based sauces, or full blown meats topping my pie. Now, with the extra prices garnered from toppings, it's generally easier to order a specialty pizza and simply modify it to be vegan. That being the case, I can see where a cook might make the wrong assumptions based on the name of the order and mess it up somehow. Or, you know, any number things. Maybe it was an off day, maybe they just forgot. But three times? You know way they say: three strikes, and you're out, Noble Pie. 

This pizza parlor isn't a bad place, and its clientele is generally a loyal, dedicated bunch, and I know many people that love this place. If you are willing to try it out, you probably won't be disappointed. But in my own experience, it just seems like this place is attempting to emulate the great vegan-friendly, new age pizza parlors of Portland, OR and other such cities--only they have not, in my opinion, succeeded.

I went here today for bikini waxing services. I don't think I'll go back. 

When I walked in, I hate to say it, but the place kind of smelled like a dog grooming salon. I wonder if they have ventilation issues or something. It was aesthetically very pretty and looked clean, but I was a bit put off by the smell. The receptionist was busy checking out other clients and talking with someone she appeared to be friends with, so it took a minute to get me checked in.  I wasn't really warmly greeted and the receptionist went right back to talking to her friend rather than welcoming me, a new client.

I was on time for my waxing appointment, and the waxer was running behind, but no one bothered to tell me, or even check in to see how I was doing during my wait or apologize for not running on schedule. No one asked me to take a seat or offered me any coffee or water from their refreshment area until a random stylist came up to me after I had been waiting for about 10 minutes already. 

When my waxer came out, she was visibly flustered because she was running behind. I kind of felt bad for her. Granted, I was using a Groupon for waxing services so I'm sure that's why she was so busy. She was very nice throughout the whole appointment.

She led me into the waxing room, which was nice looking and private. She had me take off my shoes and pants with her in the room, which I thought was a little strange. When I have gotten waxed before  I was given a few minutes of privacy to do this. 

She had me leave may panties on to wax as well. I guess some people do it that way, but again, I had always had my knickers off before when having this service. Then came the reason I won't return: She used the same metal spatula to apply all my wax and was "double dipping" in the wax pot. If I wasn't in such a rush to get this done for a special occasion and I hadn't bought the groupon already, I would have ended the appointment. That is extremely unhygenic. Now I get to spend the next week or so praying that I don't get a skin infection or anything. I was also bruised just a bit, but not much. My waxer also told me her last 2 appointments directly before me were also for bikini services, so all I was thinking the whole time was "ew" and "man, I hope those other 2 girls showered as thoroughly as I did before their appointments."

I can't speak for their other salon services, but for what they charge for a wax, to be treated the way I was and for the waxing to be unhygenic like that I feel ripped off. I'll probably call and complain about the 'double dipping,' because that just shouldn't EVER happen. The only reason this place gets 2 stars is because it did look nice, the waiting area was comfortable, and my waxer was very sweet and friendly.

EDIT: I called the salon and expressed my concerns about the waxing method. My waxer called me back promptly and informed me that they use NuFree waxing product, which is 'self sanitizing,' allowing them to use one spatula per client (I did forget to mention a new, clean spatula was used on me). I did look it up online and was able to find a scientific published study that seems to back up this claim. Still, based on my other experiences there, I don't know that I would go back.

Ambiance: this is where this restaurant really shines. This place is impressive on the inside, warm, charming, romantic, inviting, and very well done. 

Food: We started with the fried chicken wings. They were certainly good, but I've had better. Somewhat forgettable. Just ordinary breaded wings to me. The sour cream and onion sauce was way too mayo-y to me as well. 

Then, we moved on to share several dinner entree items:
 - Steak and Fries: a very nice quality skirt steak and decent fries. Steak was under-salted and therefore a bit bland but easily remedied. Their signature ketchup was very good too.
 - Octopus: very, very good, tender, and nice flavor kick from the kalamata olives. 
 - Wild Boar Ribs: biggest disappointment. Did not remotely approach your standard baby back ribs flavor, richness, and tenderness. These were somewhat chewy, dry, and the bbq sauce is just all wrong. The jalapeño corn bread was good though. 
 - Hamburger: very good, though relatively small for a double patty burger. Anyhow, clearly one of their fortes. 
 - Mac & Cheese: more like Mac & Cream Sauce. Meh. Was decent, I've had much, much better.
 - Baked Beans: Tasted fresh, firm, and nicely balanced sweet sauce with savory bacon. 
 - Sautéed Greens: I think this had bok choy mostly. It was clearly sautéed in butter and garlic, leaving it tasty if not too greasy from the butter. 
 - Baked Cookie dessert: what a missed opportunity. This could have been the start of the night, instead tasting like a reheated, stale old cookie with the inexcusably tiniest scoop of ice-cream ever.  Should have been more chocolaty, more tender, of ooey gooey goodness!

Summary: 
At the prices they charge, we expected more. Pretty good overall, not good enough at these prices. 

disclaimer: however harsh my review may seem, my main goal is to be completely honest to both the business owner and to fellow Yelper's, as that is what I would want myself. In the end, I wish every restaurant great success! I know its a very tough business!

text:
Visited this restaurant with three friends for the first time to take advantage of a Groupon coupon. Out of the 4 of us, one person hated it, one liked it and the other two thought it was "ok". None of us was blown away. Service was average.

We started out with caipirinhas. They were delicious and the limes were very fresh. It was the perfect start to the evening. We ordered a few appetizers - the empanadas de bife (beef empanadas) came in an order of 3 and were very bland. They were served with a "spicy" tomato sauce that was not very spicy or flavorful, although it tasted of plain fresh tomatoes. We had aipim frito, or fried yucca, which was also disappointingly bland and dry. 

Then the entrees came... Two of us ordered the National dish (Feijoada de Ogum) , which had been highly recommended and even posted in a local foodie site as one of the best comfort foods St. Louis has to offer. It was a very large portion - served in a large bowl, with a plate of rice, greens, oranges and farofa (a dry yucca flour). You are supposed to mix the large bowl contents (black bean stew with sausage and pork ribs) into the rice, greens and farofa mix. The oranges were dry and not very tasty. The mix tasted good and unique at first, but became boringly bland the more I ate. The pieces of pork rib (part of the bean, sausage and rib stew) were seared on the outside but very rare and bloody inside, making for a very unpleasant texture when mixed with the other parts of the stew. This was an ok meal, but the best I could say about the national dish is that it is "average" and too bland and boring to eat the whole thing. The other person that ordered it absolutely hated it.  Something tells me I should have tried something else from the menu despite the "national dish" label.

One of the people in our party ordered the bobo de camarao (jumbo shrimp in a creamy coconut and spicy yucca sauce). She really liked it, although was disappointed that the shrimp had tails and veins on them and after a while, she felt the sauce was also a bit boring to finish the whole dish. 

The last person in our party had beef kabobs. He said they were good, but that he's had much better elsewhere and, although the meat tasted fresh, it was underwhelming in terms of seasonings. It was served with rice and vegetables, which were reminiscent of side dishes in an old folks diner. 

Finally we ordered desserts. We tried all three desserts on the menu. The coconut bread pudding was by far the best of the three and probably the best overall dish of the night, with the flan coming in a close second.

We were quite surprised when we heard the server offer a nearby table some specials that were never offered to us, even though it was the same server who had taken care of us.  

Overall, the ambiance was very nice and the decor was great, but the 
food let us a bit underwhelmed despite having great expectations. The prices are reasonable ($6-8 for appetizers ; 18-23 for entrees) but for the averageness of our meal, the $35 groupon coupon was a very welcome discount.
llama_8b_pred_reasoning: The models show moderate agreement with a final star of 3, with BERT being the most confident at 2 stars. However, the review text suggests that the food was 'average' and the prices were reasonable, with the groupon coupon being a welcome discount, which aligns with a 3-star rating.

Within 2 hours of the installation I noticed a change in symptoms. Three weeks have passed and I'm still breathing easy!

After such a good experience, I requested the installation of a whole-house humidifier, as the one I had was 30 years old and non-functioning, creating excess static electricity throughout the house. I noticed a gap in the tubing from the humidifier and Ben sent someone out quickly to fix the issue. Everything is working well now.

I highly recommend you choose Ben and his team to address your HVAC issues. He has integrity, is very knowledgeable, and takes the time to explain options thoroughly. When you have someone working on such a critical piece of your home's infrastructure, this is exactly what you want.

text:
On a rare visit to downtown Sparks, glowing sign of newly opened Golden Rotisserie beckoned with the promise of marinated, spit-roasted meat. It's a counter service place with simple furnishings, but plenty of room for a family meal.

Despite having never visited their original Truckee location, I was immediately struck with deja vu. The menu is eerily similar to that of much-lauded T's Mesquite Rotisserie in Incline Village. When asked about that, the guy at the counter shrugged his shoulders, and said, "I don't know." Fair enough.

A large rotisserie dominates the small, open kitchen space, though it appears it's only loaded up with beef tri-tip, chicken, and pork shoulder in the morning, then "held hot" to be served as burritos, tacos, tostadas, quesadillas, and sandwiches. Or, you can order a quarter or half pound serving of meat with a choice of two sides: cucumber salad, black beans, spanish rice, potato salad, and coleslaw. Like I said, deja vu all over again.

The "daily special" trio of tacos al pastor ($7.50) was served in the traditional manner, a pair of small corn tortillas supporting a decent amount of meat, topped with plenty of fresh onion and cilantro. They were served with rice and beans, lime wedges, and a two ounce cup of salsa (choice of mild, medium, or hot).

The beans were a little soupy, but the slightly salty flavor was pretty good. The rice had plenty of lime and cilantro. Unfortunately, the telltale pineapple flavor of al pastor was completely absent, replaced by crunchy, charred, bitterness that even a healthy dose of medium salsa couldn't improve. I chose not to finish them.

My friend's chile relleno burrito ($8.50) was full of black beans, rice, guacamole, lettuce, and sour cream, with the stuffed mild pepper in the center. It was really tasty even before the addition of hot salsa, though strangely lacking in cheese. Further inspection showed a thin layer inside the pepper, so perhaps "stuffed" isn't the word.

Meat plates come with a choice of corn tortillas or a slab of garlic bread grilled with plenty of butter and garlic. The bread was a nice addition to a half-pound order of tri-tip ($11.50) with potato salad and beans. The sweet salad could do with more seasoning and less dressing, but the beef? Oh man. Marinated in a mixture of honey, soy, and lime, the large slices were tender, delicious, and surprisingly moist. It would definitely make a great steak sandwich, and was easily the high point of our visit.

Although a half pound plate of soy lime chicken ($9.50) may have been dynamite when it came off the spit, by dinner time it was a mushy, dry disappointment. The skin was still acceptably crispy, and the marinade flavor was pretty decent. Sure, the meat came easily off the bone, but the breast quarter was drier than a cheap,  frozen turkey left too long in the oven. The attached wing was essentially inedible jerky. The dark meat quarter fared better, but only just. The sides of nicely seasoned coleslaw and marinated salad of cucumber, carrot, and onion were pretty enjoyable. I'm tempted to see if the chicken is better at lunch, but I'd probably just give in to that drool-worthy tri-tip.

The waiter came back 5 minutes later and told me "I'm sorry but we don't have any olive oil"

He said this nicely but without a hint of awareness as to the extraordinary absurdity of this statement. I asked him bewilderedly "you don't have olive oil?" And he said, "Well sometimes we have it but we ran out"

 This is 4pm on a Friday before a busy weekend on Decatur street and this is an Italian restaurant that has allowed themselves to run out of, of all things....olive oil.

I said "um... Ok well how about any kind of oil? Canola maybe? Or margarine?" He said he would see what he could do.

He came back to the table with a bowl of red beans and rice with 2 pieces of toast on top and fully touching.  He placed the bowl in front of my freind and gave me a small dish and said "here's some scallion oil, is that ok?" And I accepted it . It took me more than a few seconds to process what he had said.... I said pointing to the bowl in front of my freind "Oh... that's MY toast?" 

He said "yes!.. Very cheerily too I must add as if there was nothing remotely wrong with the situation. I realized instantly that the gap between his reality and mine was so cavernously deep that any attitude or complaint I gave him would be utterly futile and just make us both vastly more uncomfortable than 2 pieces of toast ordered out of boredom was worth.

"Yes" I said "If that is my toast on top of his food, and I have no plate, I would like a plate for my toast"

He brought me a plate, I took the toast off my freind's bowl, we spoke no further on the subject and all was right with the world.

So....Alls I'm sayin' is.... I didn't really eat here but.... If you like olive oil, napkins and you prefer that the food you order come on it's own plate rather than stacked on top of other people food as if plates are a short-supply luxury, this Italian restaurant may not be for you.

text:
After an hour of comparing prospective birthday brunch venues, the photos, location, menu offering, and "wow" factor of Cinder House won me over, so I booked a Sunday morning reservation. Unfortunately, I'd asked them on Social Media where we could get the complimentary hot cocoa and never received a reply, but that's a thing if you're dining here, fyi. 

I also found out from a friend that Cinder House offers free valet if you're dining in their restaurant via the Four Seasons valet. 
This too would have been really useful to know prior since my friend and I walked in the frigid morning temps from our hotel all the way down there for our meal. 

Make no mistake, not only is this in the Four Seasons, it's also in possibly one of the best places to view the Arch and the Mississippi. As such, expect to pay premium prices for drinks and food. The food:

Buffett style usually isn't something I find exciting, as the visuals remind me of my subpar, pre-yelp days living in Lake Tahoe - dried out food, poor quality items to offset high waste, and overall just eating for volume to justify cost.  Cinder House reminded me really good buffets can exist, even in St. Louis. 
Arriving into the lobby, I immediately saw the few carving stations to the right, and was already happier than most of my buffet experiences. Three stations, all with minimal lines, awaited once greeting our friendly hostess. The first station had perfectly seared Ahi tuna, the second had smoked brisket and smoked pork shoulder, and the third was an omelet station with so many fixins! The meat stations both had about five sauces, mostly mexican inspired. I tried the blended green sauce and a green salsa with my tuna, which was really yummy.

For a brunch menu, I was disappointed to see half of the entire offering was baked goods/pastries, but most of them were beautiful and delicious. We found out the dishes rotate every week, according to our server, which means each time you go, it's like a new experience. From the baked goods row, I tried the pumpkin bread, chocolate pot du creme, pomegranate topped torte, a croissant, and ginger carrot cake. Surprisingly, the carrot cake was the star. The sponge was light and fluffy but spicy, and the frosting was a not too sweet cream cheese, topped with a beautiful slice of candied orange. 

Opposite to the row of baked treats were some al fresca options including smoked salmon and cream cheese, along with deviled eggs, grilled veggies, and a few salads. I was surprised to love the shaved cabbage caesar as much as I did, I highly recommend it if you enjoy dressing-heavy salads.

Being this was my only meal for the day, I went back for seconds of meat, and by my estimate, I probably had around $100 of ahi tuna alone, which wasn't my goal, but it was just so darn good. 

The fixed price brunch also included two drink tokens each, or they can be used for freshly pressed juices and smoothies, but we started with a bloody mary, then a glass of champagne. The bloody mary was decent, but nothing impressive. I don't need 87 things in my bloody but something more than a piece of celery would have been good, along with a little more spice, but it did the job. 

For my birthday, our server brought us a delicious "Happy Birthday" flan from a well-known chef, but I couldn't remember who. I just remember how balanced and silky it was, even after eating way more than I should have.

Overall, we were pretty happy for the location, the experience, the service (day of, not prior since they didn't respond to my questions) and the meats on offer.  I'd wish there was greater variety and selection of non-baked/sugary items, such as swapping some of the baked items for a few quiches or frittatas, but I understand they may not keep as well. 

While a little pricier than I'd expect to pay for a nice buffet, for an occasion or event, this would be a fun place to bring family or friends again. I hope they have that Ahi when I return!

Visited Frenchman on a Saturday and we came here because there was no cover and saw that there'd be live music in a few minutes at 7 and DJ spinning "japanese electronica" at 10.  

You probably won't find many places like this in N.O..  Me and my gal had already had dinner and were looking to drink.  They have a decent list of sakes and other japanese drinks and beers.  They also have tapas style food served on small plates, but like I said, we weren't hungry.  

The drinks are pricey.  We finally decided on a $15 300ml bottle of sake.  Unfortunately, they were out.  We got a different bottle for the same price but which sounded less appetizing.  And it was.  Then we got another bottle of sake, this time the cheap carbonated one.  It was a 250ml bottle for $12 and tasted great but I was rather disheartened when I read that the alcoholic content was 7%.  

After that quick bottle I felt really sober.  And I was, we'd already dropped $30+ and weren't even buzzed.  I started buying $5 sapporo drafts (tied for cheapest drafts they have), which were good, but after I had three and she had two and somewhere along the way I'd broken down and ordered the "seasoned octopus with wasabi" (ugh, slimy canned octopus) we'd spent over $60 with tips and were just barely scraping a buzz along.  

There were a couple reasons why we stayed there for as long as we did.  One, there was a cool black and white japanese movie being played on the top corner of a brick wall.  Two, Fi Yi Yi, the drum circle band played most of the time that we were there, which was cool, but we really wanted to hear the DJ spin jap-electronica and dance but we ran out of funds and left.  Not sure if he ever showed up.

In a way, I feel like Yukis takes advantage of their uniqueness.  Sake isn't the cheapest way to drink, especially at a bar.  It's just like buying wine at bars and restaurants, and beer for that matter; obviously it's going to cost more.  Yuki's just didn't have any reasonably good sounding cheap options.  Except maybe the one they were out of.  And then their beer is expensive as well.  I just can't warrant that kind of expense for half of a mediocre buzz.  Maybe they think that because they have food they can charge restaurant prices for booze.  Or maybe that's just Frenchman St. for you.  I don't know yet, I'm new here.  

Left at midnight and went home feeling too sober and broke.  And my bum hurt because those red stools are uncomfortable.

Will I be back?  Probably, because I don't learn well from my mistakes.  That and I like sake and Japanese kietsch.  Next time I'll just make sure I'm drunk first.

Regarding the star rating, it's tough because there were two things that were terribly wrong with our meals at our visit to Bardenay, but everything else was just fine.
Maybe not "fine." The service was lacking. We had a seat on the nice patio during the end of the lunch hour, and everything moved particularly slowly. The patio was almost full, but the inside was nearly empty, so there wasn't much of an excuse there.
And the niceties of the patio and this restaurant's immaculate interior are really its saving grace. Being on Grove Street in the Basque Block with a nice building though, I don't think, warrants a positive review in itself. The food is really what makes an experience excel over a location, regardless of the latter being a plus or not.
The two things that went wrong with this meal were food-related. First, I got a chorizo sandwich with fries. The chorizo was not as good as what I had eaten at Bar Gernika the night before, but was certainly still pretty good and the bread was really nice. The fries, however, were off. When I asked, the server freely admitted that they were the frozen/Sysco variety. WTF? This is Idaho! Does any respectable restaurant really need to subject their customers to frozen french fries? And not only frozen fries, Sysco fries. I mean, I'm not looking for the Bittercreek Ale House standard of excellent housemade fries, I'm just looking for something that I can't buy in a big bag at the supermarket for $2. And the only reason I know what these fries are is because, for years in college, I ate them at Burger King until I got disgusted with them and can't eat them anymore. No, seriously, these are the same fries as you find at Burger King. There's just no reason for that.
Okay, so maybe I shouldn't automatically expect fresh fries at an Idaho restaurant. I mean, it's the Gem State and not the Fresh-Cut Potato State. But the other bad part of the meal was inexcusable. My companion got an "ahi" tuna salad. Quote marks are necessary there because it was nothing like the ahi tuna you may be used to. This was, essentially, the tuna that comes out of the bag. It tasted and looked no different. This is, admittedly, one step above the Bumblebee variety, coated with brine, mayonnaise and a "lord knows" variety of chemicals, but it still sucked and rendered the salad virtually inedible because of the tuna's outright stench.
So we left with finishing only about 1/2 of our meals. I would not return here, nor would I recommend it to anyone else. If you want Basque, go to Bar Gernika or the Basque Market next door.

I was excited to see Jody Charles expand his pop-up festival and catering business and open Louisiana Soul Bayou at the Chow Public Market.

I ordered a bowl of chicken and sausage gumbo and a shrimp po-boy and fried okra.

An old Louisiana adage is that first you make a roux. The combination of equal parts flour and oil are typically cooked to a dark brown and then combined with the trinity of onions, bell peppers and celery. It adds depth to the flavor of a dish and acts as a thickener.

The gumbo at Louisiana Soul Bayou lacked that depth. The broth was watery and there was little flavor outside of the chicken and sausage. The vegetables didn't appear to have been sweated, so they didn't incorporate into the dish.

Cajun dishes don't have to be firery hot, but they must be flavorful and heavily seasoned. The gumbo lacked that kind of flavor. Judged against thosec11 bowls of gumbo I ate in Louisiana, all of which were great, this one fell far short.

It's unfair to judge a Louisiana po-boy against one made anywhere else. You can't get the special bread from John Gendusa Bakery or Leidenheimer Baking Co. anywhere else. A thin, crispy crust and pillowy goodness inside. A hoagie loaf just doesn't measure up.

If I hadn't been spoiled by the shrimp po-boys at Zimmer's Seafood next to Gendusa's in the Gentilly neighborhood of New Orleans or at Liuza's by the Track, then the Louisiana Soul Bayou one would have been fine. There wasn't any seasoning, so it was a little bland.

I love okra, but again their fried okra didn't appear to have been seasoned so it lacked flavor.

The staff was friendly and I hope Jody can tweak his recipes and come up with a winning concept that can thrive here.

I absolutely LOOOVE this place!! Yes, it's true that Franklin Fountain is a go-to tourist dessert shop in Philadelphia, but for good reason. The ice cream flavors are unique and the employees are so nice, helpful, and accommodating. Even the layout and ambiance of the shop is unique, cute, and fits right into the Old City vibe. Their flavors are perfect for any type of sweet tooth here - so many flavors ranging from classic and traditional to unique and different. The location is also very convenient since it's right next to the 2nd street stop on the SEPTA blue line and is right off of Penn's Landing. 

Now to talk about the flavors. The Green Tea and the Black Raspberry are my absolute FAVORITE. I've never had better or creamier ice cream before, and all of the flavors that I've tried are just so deliciously rich and satisfying. My sister, who absolutely adores ice cream, really recommends the Hydrox Cookie (basically Franklin Fountain's take on cookies and cream ice cream) and the Peach ice cream.

There is also quite a wide selection of sundaes for those ice cream maniacs. The sundaes and specialty orders are quite expensive - more than $10 a pop - but they are definitely something special. I've tried the Mt. Vesuvius sundae, which is an absolute treat for chocolate lovers. It's quite an extravagant mix of ice cream, brownies, hot fudge, and whipped cream. Though I would highly recommend sharing this sundae since it's huge, I thought it was one of the best desserts I've ever had.

So my one main complaint really has to do with the price. Though the servings are large, I still would prefer not to pay over $5 for a small cup of ice cream or over $10 (the price of a meal!) for a sundae. If the prices were a little more reasonable, I would definitely try to stop by for ice cream a little more often.

I take all of my visiting friends and family here, and I haven't heard anything but good feedback from everyone. You can't go wrong with Franklin Fountain ice cream!

This was not a good pizza for me. Everyone has a different preference for their pie, but when requests are not honored, the problem goes deeper than lack of real experience with a classic American comfort food. Everything else on the menu may be great, but the pizza reheat was not.

I noticed they had a solid 4 star status.

When I arrived, I was curious about how long they were in that location, and the gal said 5 years.

It was hot enough, but pretty greasy, and it was full of too much cabbage and not really any other type of vegetable. It didn't have a whole lot of flavor either. I had asked on the phone what they put in their lo mein, and she said a few veggies like cabbage and green onions -  and of course chicken.  
I made the mistake of ordering the larger size not realizing that when I received it, it was enough to probably feed me for a week. That's no fault of theirs because I feel I definitely got more than enough food for the money I paid. The container was literally stuffed / jam packed with mostly noodles to the top; with no air room to spare.  


As much as 3 stars can be satisfactory (basically a C -ish average), and is also a somewhat respectable rating for most restaurants of this type, if I do end up going back again, I will end up trying something else without boatloads of noodles like ex : chicken broccoli.  If it ends up tasting better, I can certainly see my review being upgraded and potentially changed to 4 stars.

Okay, Yelpers, these reviews reeally let me down.  Being from California and having the same dentist nearly all my life, (I've seen two other dentists that have been fine) I had hoped this would be a one-stop shop after reading reviews, but nah.

My first visit was fine, a breeze even.  The front desk staff is friendly and pleasant, and the place is clean.  I was seen on time and felt okay about how things went.  I expressed my complaint as having pain on the lower right side.  Xrays showed that that tooth is growing in awkwardly, pushing against the tooth in front of it creating a pocket of sort. The doctor explained how pain works.  In a nutshell, he says the pain is likely coming from the top right side because there are two visible problem teeth--it simply FEELS like the bottom.  I confirm that I have had some "zings" of pain up there, but most of my pain is on the bottom. I remember specifically saying, "it's weird, it doesn't really feel like the pain associated with having a cavity."  It was easy to accept his theory on how pain worked because I knew with certainty it wasn't a cavity.  I'm prescribed antibiotics and schedule two extractions for a week later for the top right side, per his medical advice.   Upon taking the antibiotics, the pain never stops!  Mind you, this isn't my first extraction or infection, so when the pain is still pretty constant, I deduce that there is no infection. The way pain works is probably true, but not applicable.  It's the bottom right. Like I said initially. Still in full blown pain.   So I go back for the extractions and say I want to have the bottom right extracted instead because the antibiotics didn't work, pain still constant, yaddah yaddah yaddah. He pulls the xrays up again, reads the notes he wrote in my chart and insists we move forward with the two extractions he suggested.  This is where I take FULL RESPONSIBILITY for staying. At that point, I should've hightailed it outta there and gone for a second opinion. Instead, I laid back and settled in. :-(  Minus One Star for Lack of Attentiveness/Bullying

Here's where it gets sticky. I mean bloody. I mean, you get it.  I get numbed up with shots and ointment and Doctor Michael Leggio dives right in. The first extraction was a piece of cake. The tooth had fallen out some years back and only needed the remaining tooth to be removed and thoroughly cleaned out.  He wasn't the most gentle, but that's nothing I couldn't deal with.  Suddenly, painfully, I feel my lip being ripped/split open.  He was standing behind me, and I swear he had his hands all over my dang face.  My mouth obvi, was wide open, & having his hands positioned that way, caused a tiny, painful laceration from pulling at my teeth one way and my face the other. It hurt when it happened, I definitely felt every bit of the tear, but by the time I got home and started looking, I couldn't see or even feel it. I assumed it was so tiny that it had simply healed already. WRONG. Once the shots wore off, there it was.  You had better believe that thing got progressively worse living inside my wet, inner lip.  See photo for grossness. Minus One Star for Pain & Suffering Due to Face Damage.

On to the second tooth--the doozie apparently. Leggio is doing his job and the inevitable drool arises and starts to trickle.  It ran down my chin, down my neck, over my shoulder, and onto my back.  That's some rapid moving spit, isn't it? The RDA, Marsha is sitting there doing god knows what. Whatever it was, it must have been more important than chasing saliva. Nonetheless, I give her the benefit of the doubt--maybe this saliva is still clear and not bloodied? Perhaps that's why she hadn't noticed it? My mouth HAD to have been filled up with spit for it to eventually spill over, right?  Dah well, I'm numb, maybe not. So I struggle from underneath the bib thing & wipe it myself.  In fact, to my surprise, it's up to me to wipe my own drool for the duration of my visit. At this point, I'm absolutely flabbergasted. One, how in the hell is this woman still employed? Two, why in the hell wouldn't Leggio wake her a$$ up? (I shared this experience with my RDA niece and boy was she disgusted) Minus One Star for Negligence/Sleeping On the Job/Acting Like I Aint Sh!t

Now here I am, three weeks + hundreds of dollars later and what do ya know?   My gums surrounding that lower bottom right tooth are now INFLAMED, SWOLLEN, THROBBING & STILL IN PAIN. So swollen that it hits the top teeth when I chew. I've found myself literally holding my mouth slightly open--there's no such thing as having a comfortably closed mouth at this point. ugh.  Minus One Star for Time & Money Wasted + Problem Unresolved.

Final Answer:  I went in for a service, and that service was provided.  The experience, tho, was a nightmare.  Also note, if I wasn't such a team player, I would've had my phone out despite the signage and captured a dirty mouthwash cup. Another win for dear old Marsha. Stay away, guys.

My wife and I went to Marigold tonight after being told how amazing it was (and seeing the #2 ranking in Philly Mag) and we were let down.

Finally, we thought both our desserts (my wife had Going Bananas and I had the Chocolate in Many Forms) were huge let-downs. 

In the end, the food runs from very tasty to not very tasty. It's clear they are doing some really adventurous things, but given the prices, I think they should hit more often than they do, and their misses should not be as big as they were, and they could really work on their service. 

Marigold Kitchen is an interesting idea, but it's nowhere near the second best restaurant in Philly. My rating is somewhere in between two and three stars.

Apart from the host, the service was prompt, friendly, and attentive. My meal sat at $17 after tax and tip -- and that's after I intentionally eschewed even the entry-level margaritas (which ring in at $10). However, the food filled our empty, hungover bellies and the water was a godsend before heading back into the brutal heat...I just hate to waste a meal in Nawlin's on sub-par po'boys!

text:
So, this is The Nations, huh? Interesting. After being gone for so long, I have a hard time remembering if certain areas of the city (or, outside the city as this area technically is) had names/designations or if this is an outgrowth of population explosions, search for housing and what not. Whatever the reason, increased interest/activity in urban renewal* is usually a good thing. So, The Nations... and The Stone Fox.

I'd heard much about this out-of-the-way spot long before coming here and am pleased to note that it lived up to its billing. It's moody, interesting, fun, and full of potential. Kudos to the owners for having the vision and concept. And kudos, also, for having a 2 for 1 beer special going on with Bingo on a quiet Monday night. I can dig it. And, I should dig it, given the '70s throwbacks throughout the air and on the walls. $3 well drinks made things go down pretty easily, as well. Being that I was hungry as well as thirsty, I studied the menu for some choice eats. I almost went to town on the black bean chicken chili nachos (right? how good does that sound?) but our waitress talked me in to the comparatively healthy chickpea/beet veggie burger... which I, then, proceeded to make unhealthy by 'Elising' it with bbq sauce, onion ring, pickles, cheddar cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, and avocado topping. Of course, it was magically delicious. How could anything *not* be with all those amazing toppings. The veggie burger itself was a bit crumbly but that's par for the course with homemade veggie burgers.

Food coma starting, I got my second of the 2 for 1 beer and walked around a bit. The dj was spinning '70s tunes on vinyl. The bartender was doing some interesting things behind the bar. But my attention was held by the deck. This wooden charmer was made for warm weather and cold beer. I'll be back for it. There are a lot of good things going on at The Stone Fox. Regardless of where you live in the metro area, hop on over and give it a spin. 

*Let's keep it responsible.

There is a little something for everyone at Lettuce Lake Park.  

We visited yesterday as part of the Hillsborough County Hiking Spree. After paying the two dollar entrance fee we parked in one of the paved parking lots right inside the entrance. From here we had access to the playground, which we visited first for my five-year-olds sake, the paved hiking/biking/jogging loop and the rentable pavilions.

The playground consists of a couple swings and a structure that has lots of slides coming from it. It is pretty standard as far as Hillsborough County Park playgrounds go. What I liked about this one is that the playground is located in a huge open area. So not only can kids swing and slide but they can also run, break out a soccer game, play baseball or any number of other activities that require more space. 

After we were through with the playground, it was time to get our hike on. We started at the paved loop that runs around the entire park. The loop is a pretty easy walk. It has workout equipment at various stops along it. Some of the equipment is pretty obvious as far as what it should be used for (pull up bars, gymnastic rings) and some of it, if you aren't in the know, requires imagination. I've seen some parks that have little signs explaining the different workout areas or offering suggested workouts and I think Lettuce Lake could use that. From the loop there are a number of "trails" that lead off of it. We left the loop to take a look at a circle of cypress trees in the swamp. We also left it to spend time on the boardwalk

The boardwalk is probably the best part of hiking at Lettuce Lake. From the safety of this boardwalk you can look out into the Hillsborough River. text:
We've heard from a few people that around this area that this place was good.  Since we happened to be in the small town of Souderton we decided to stop in for lunch.  We made a reservation (through Resy), since I hate waiting.  Surprisingly the spots filled pretty quickly, from when my wife checked them to a half an hour later they were nearly booked a few hours out.  That's good for them!

I was surprised to see a smoker in the back of the restaurant with someone putting full racks of ribs on it.  It's definitely a legit smoker, they have the wood stacked nearby and the ribs from where I was standing looked to be St. Louis style ribs.  

The restaurant is nice inside.  It's clean, well laid out and has a good atmosphere.  We got a table on the patio which is fully enclosed and heated.  Due to covid, there were a lot of tables they weren't able to use, so we couldn't grab a seat by the bar (which I prefer).  

The staff were all very friendly and did a great job.  They definitely work as a team which makes our experience better.  

I grabbed a Yards in a can, but they do have a pretty impressive drink list.  This location is part of Boardroom Spirits so all of the alcohol was from BR.  

We came for the pizza, but their menu was more than just that.  I'm not quite sure how to categorize it...it's not a pizza place, it's not a bbq place, it's not a burger place or a salad place; but they offer all of that.

We ordered the Pulled Pork Nachos and the Detroit Style Pepperoni pizza.  The nachos were okay, they honestly would've been better without the pork.  The pork wasn't bad, it just didn't have flavor.  If something is called "smoked", I want to taste smoke and with their offset smoker setup they can definitely bring some flavor.  The cheese on the nachos was good as was the seasoning they put on their chips.  The toppings aside from the pork were good too.  I probably wouldn't order again if I returned.  

The pizza came out and looked great.  I have high expectations for what people call Detroit style...I'm from Detroit and have been eating this stuff before the "foodie" community was even born.  It looked good upon arrival, the cheese was crusted around the edge, the pepperoni had crisped up, the sauce was on top and there was grated parmesan (although more than I would usually expect.  And finally, there was a chiffonade of basil...something I wasn't excited about as I find it can be pretty over powering and if bruised during prep it's way too over powering. 

Took a bite and I was intrigued, the dough was crips along the outside but pillowy soft in the crumb.  The sauce was perfect, a little sweet but not much and it was room temp, not cold, not hot...perfect!  But then the basil, it was delicate, not over powering as I expected and the flavor of it is exactly what a pizza like this needs to cut through the richness of it.  

The pizza is small, only four pieces so if you're hungry or feeding a group get a few.  It's $14 which when you think about it, if you split it, you spent $7 on a very good lunch.  Plus the smaller size means there's less to take home.  

Overall I would definitely return to Northbound.  I want to try some of their cocktails, I want to try some of the other pizzas and some of their ribs.  I'm hoping the nachos were a one off.  But even if everything else on the menu was as underwhelming as the nachos...the pizza makes it worth the visit.

Lots of smoothie choices that will make you feel healthy AF.

I've recently gone on a total smoothie kick. I realized that the only way I'm going to consume vegetables is if it is in liquid form so I can inhale it quickly. Enter Xtreme Juice. After reading a whole lot of reviews from Tampa Bay Yelpers I trust (thank you Elites!) I decided to make the foray into South Tampa to try this place.

After reading that the lines can get ridiculously long, I decided to go when I figured nobody would be there, at 10:30 a.m. on a Monday. Too late for breakfast, pretty early for lunch, I figured it was a safe bet. Well, there wasn't a line, but there was still a pretty steady stream of people. When I got there, there were three people waiting on their drink and while I waited for mine, four more people arrived. When you're serving what the people want, you don't get a downtime!

I'm so glad I looked at the menu (and read reviews) before I went. They have a massive menu! Luckily, since I'm basically drinking smoothies to consume veggies, I was able to rule out a majority of the menu. I was torn between the Liquid Gold and the Hail to the Kale. Honestly, before I arrived I decided on the Liquid Gold, but somehow completely forgot when seeing the overwhelmingly vast menu and went with the Hail to the Kale because it was first on the menu board. I was mentally kicking myself after, but I noticed that it had an icon next to it signifying it is a customer favorite. I forgave myself a little after that.

Service was pretty fast. It is a small store so I can see it getting claustrophobic if you have to wait and there is a long line. If you don't' like crowds then you'll definitely want to come on an off time. 

I enjoyed the Hail to the Kale. It was a little tart and I felt healthy AF drinking it. The 16 oz was the perfect size for me. If you're looking for a sweet, creamy smoothie, this isn't it, but if you're looking to get your greens in and feel like a beast (in a good way), this is an enjoyable way to do so. 

The veggie smoothies do cost about $3 more than fruit smoothies (my aching heart), but I bet the ingredients are more expensive. 

I'll definitely stick to making my own smoothies because of smoothie prices alone, but when I want to step out of my comfort zone, this is a great place to do so.

text:
Like the other *very few* non 5-star reviews, I feel that I must lead with a preface. I do not discredit any awards this restaurant has won or knock Chef Shaya for any reason. However, if I force myself to be completely objective, I believe 4 stars is an accurate reflection of my dining experience. 

My husband made a reservation 2 months ago for a Saturday night dinner and the day finally came for us to dine here! I would say reservations are totally necessary here unless you are fine with bar seating (which to me seemed crowded) but I was also informed there is a courtyard open on good weather days that does not require reservations (didn't see this space for myself). 

A quick glance around the restaurant revealed a full house filled with parties of all sizes, no kids/teens, and glasses of wine on almost every table. It's a very 'sexy restaurant'--dark, beautiful lighting, upbeat music, and plates intended to be shared...a tad on the loud side. Our server stopped by promptly asking if we had any questions about the menu and to take our drink orders. We ordered the lamb kebab from the small plates section, three selections from the 'for the table' section (3 for $15 special), and the cauliflower hummus. 

The plates arrived in shifts which was fine but the lamb kebab was seriously delayed--I politely reminded our server that we had ordered the lamb since we had finished our other plates and she said that the dishes come out in courses. It just seemed odd that something from the small plates (which I took to mean appetizers) would come out last. But as far as the taste, the lamb was tender and flavorful similar to lamb at other Mediterranean places. You get two "links" of lamb in the order. 

For the 3 for $15 dishes, we chose the shipka peppers, the baba ghanoush, and the Israeli salad. I was disappointed in the shipka peppers as they were essentially bell papers filled with goat cheese; I love goat cheese but was just now wowed by the dish. You get two peppers in the order. The baba ghanoush and Israeli salad were tasty, also similar to other Mediterranean restaurants in the city.

The cauliflower hummus was very good but I must point out that it is not hummus made out of cauliflower (don't know if that is obvious or not). Instead, it is nicely seasoned and spiced cauliflower atop hummus. The best comparison I can make is that the cauliflower was very similar to Indian aloo gobi. Very tasty and my second favorite selection of the evening.

My most favorite thing you ask? The pita! Seriously, the pita is as fluffy as a pillow! So warm, delicious, chewy, carb-y, just perfection. The servers bring you a pita at a time and eating with your hands is totally allowed (err..we did at least). There was a point in the evening where we were pita-less for almost 10 minutes before someone brought us another one. Diners definitely need constant pita supply for all of the hummus-trimmed dishes!

We enjoyed the food and will definitely come back. I just think I got bit by the very high expectation bug on this one!

text:
Nan will always be my favorite restaurant in Philadelphia.

My best friend and I found this gem on a Thursday night about two years ago. We were really hungry and we were looking for cheap eats. From the outside decor, we thought Nan would be the perfect place for a quick bite in a somewhat sketchy looking restaurant.

Lo and behold our great surprise when we entered and it was gorgeous. It's a quaint place, great for couples but also very accommodating for groups as well. My friend and I were quickly seated and menus were graciously brought to us by the owner of the restaurant. 

The first time we went, I tried the duck and my friend tried a crab dish. Honestly we don't remember exactly what they were called but it was highly recommended and we just went for it.

Hands down, some of the best food I've ever tasted. We fell in love.
And then we found out that it was a BYOB. Cue the wedding bells, we decided that this was going to our monthly place and we were never going to cheat on it.

My friend and I go there monthly, we always get seated by the same waiter who is also the owner, we always bring a bottle of champagne, and we always order the special of the day. We have never been disappointed.

I can say that it is a bit pricey. Dinner usually rounds out to about 80-100 dollars for the two of us but it's honestly VERY very well deserved. Excellent customer service, and excellent food. Will always be our favorite and our cherished tradition.

I hope Nan never renovates its outside decor because too many people would storm our hidden gem.

For my inaugural visit to NOLA, it sure was nice to end our two week Caribbean vacation at The Ritz Carlton New Orleans. 

LOCATION:
The utmost convenience as they're on Canal Street just one block from the start of Bourbon Street's busy stretch.  There are tons of restaurants and shops nearby within walking distance. 

ATMOSPHERE:
It's your typical marble-laden Ritz Carlton.  The main lobby and registration desk are on the second floor, forcing you to use the elevators twice in order to access your room.  A beautiful courtyard sits off the lobby & lounge that's decorated with beautiful foliage surrounded by the hotel on all four sides. 

ROOM:
We overlooked the center courtyard with a sliver view of the mighty Mississippi, though there are no balconies here.  Decor was very inviting with warm colors, rich designs and exquisite fabrics.  Sleep quality was good with a strong a/c, comfortable bed & pillows, quiet rooms and all the usual amenities.  The ice machine is near the elevators.  Oddly you still pay for Wi-Fi here and charging ports were lacking. 

BATHROOM:
Single basin, shower-tub combo and enclosed lavatory.  Water pressure was strong with fast drainage.  The amenities are very perfume-y but luckily my home-brought stash was still full so no problems here. 

DAVENPORT LOUNGE:
We retired one evening to the jazz sounds of Jeremy Davenport, the headliner the lounge is named after.  Drinks were pricey but this is The Ritz.  The lounge also hosts twice daily tea service. 

SERVICE:
The only staff I interacted with were two friendly housekeepers that were tending to our room as we returned at an odd time.  I'm sure we were a breath of fresh air for them from the usual stuffy guests they have to deal with.  

TIPS:
Be sure to try the complimentary gumbo cart stationed across the front desk in the afternoon time.  The gumbo was amazingly delish but sadly ruined all other gumbo experiences for me in the city.  A take home copy of the recipe is located in the room, but I have yet to attempt it.  

There is a short cut to Bourbon Street without having to use the main entrance on Canal Street.  From the lobby, walk through the Davenport Lounge and take the elevators to the first level.  You'll end up near the meeting rooms which lets you out on the corner of Dauphine & Iberville.  Coming back in requires key access. 

OVERALL:
There isn't anything as rewarding as coming back to a high end hotel after a long, hot, humid, sticky day in the Big Easy.

Bourbon Street and the Bayou with a Brooklyn sensibility

If this place isn't a local landmark, it should be. Galliano brings the bistro treatment to the indigenous cuisine of Louisiana. 

From an outsider perspective, it is admittedly hard to know what constitutes authentic Louisiana cuisine, but I know delicious food and this place most certainly has it. 

The gumbo, to me, is the standout. It comes boiling hot in a little cauldron that would singe the hairs on your arm if it got too close. Also noteworthy are the duck wings -- succulent and tender with a sauce that curious mix of Tobasco and some sort of Szechuan flavor. The stuffed pork chop that I coveted and stole from my friend's plate had the smokiness of good BBQ brisket but without the fattiness. The Sunday pot roast was completely unexpected. Being a Bostonian, I have a preconceived notion of what a pot roast is -- you know, the "Yankee" kind. This was an unexpected riff on the classic with dirty rice, something called "poor man's gravy" that was plenty rich for me, and bits of what I think were sweet potatoes. It was tender and delicious. The desserts are worth saving room for, I recommend either the Cherries Jubilee (yay, fire!) or the peanut butter cup cake. 

Galliano represents New Orleans' culinary reputation well, such that after a disappointing venture to an actual "landmark restaurant" that was so abysmal I couldn't even eat it (but that is another review),  we went back to Galliano because we knew we would leave full and happy.

Get the arepas.

text:
Friends and fellow Yelpers Rick and Holly Garrett are regulars at Big Mike's Cafe, partly owing to the fact that Big Mike's hosts an acoustic jam every other Monday night that they put together but also because it's close to their home and a mighty fine place for a meal. 

While I've not yet made it over for Monday nights, I finally found myself in the neighborhood on a Friday after work and decided it would be a great time to try it out. 

I arrived at Big Mike's early in the dinner hour and, in fact, was the only customer when I arrived. That didn't last for long. I was greeted with a warm enthusiasm by Katie and, not surprisingly, offered my table of choice. Big Mike's is located in a small strip center next to a liquor store and in a building with a Chinese restaurant, a video retailer of some sort, and a brand new cupcake shop. Being at 96th & College, it's right on the line between Carmel and Indy and surrounded by offices. I will admit that I was mighty tempted by their pizzas, which happened to be on special tonight, but looking at the sizes concluded there was no way I could down one on my own and I really wasn't looking to take anything home. I considered their tenderloin, which Rick G. really likes, but decided to keep it simple and go for their 1/2 pound burger with cheese along with a side of your choice (I chose fries, but could have gone for slaw, chips, cottage cheese, or potato salad). The meal was $10 and it was another $1.95 for my usual unsweetened iced tea. 

The dining room is pretty simple, a nice Americana decor with oldies music (like Simon & Garfunkel) playing overhead. While it's easy to get used to the distractions that many restaurants put out there, it's kind of nice to have a restaurant you can go to and actually have a conversation. They offer a variety of other appetizers, sandwiches, and a couple of meal options. I've heard their desserts are killer, but I opted out this time around. 

The sign "Let our family, serve your family" gives you an idea of what to expect from Big Mike's, a place that also offers catering for private parties. You're going to be welcomed, remembered, and appreciated here. If they make a mistake, they're going to immediately own it and fix it (as I saw happen tonight). In short, this was a place I just plain enjoyed hanging out. 

The burger was served on a buttered pretzel bun, an interesting choice that added a distinct flavor to the beef. I won't say it's my favorite burger, but I enjoyed it and would have no problem recommending it. The fries complemented the burger well, lightly browned and having a simple yet agreeable texture. The unsweetened iced tea was terrific and served in a rather nicely sized mason jar, a jar that was so big I didn't even need my usual refill. 

When I return, and I'm pretty comfortable saying when, I find myself really wanting to try their pizza. It looks terrific. I also think this is a place I would enjoy on those nights I simply want to read and on those nights when I want to meet a friend for dinner. It has a casual, comfortable feeling to it. 

My meal came in at right about $13 plus tip. The serving sizes were good, the customer service was great, and it was an awesome way to close out a busy week. 

Big Mike's is a true family business. Katie and Mike are brother/sister, Katie specializing in the front-end and Mike being the kitchen wizard. They even feature desserts from their mother, whose desserts were popular at The Abbey (Man, I miss that place!). 

So, if you're keeping score. Good food. Great service. Local. They host local musicians. 

They're freaking awesome.

I have mixed feelings about this hotel.

They contract out this hotel to some airlines and to the FedEx trucking company, so you'll see a bunch of FedEx trucks parked on the right, backside of the parking lot.  They were my neighbors for the extend of my stay.  They check-in during the day and check-out at night.  I must say that truckers made great neighbors; never heard a peep from them.  I guess driving 8-10 hours a day can wear a guy down.  So if you're staying in the rear of the hotel, please be respectful to those truckers (they sleep during the day).


The hotel is decent.  Clean, firm beds, friendly staff, and two workstations by the check-in area for public use (complementary printing).  Free ice water with a dash of lemon by the stations.

I didn't bother to try much of the other facilities.  My time was spend mostly outdoors.  If you haven't been to Tucson before, you should really visit the national parks here.  They are quite beautiful.  (Not during the summer, of course)

My picks:

Sabino Canyon - my fav

Sanguaro National park - gates pass area is nice

Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum - a must for kids, make this your first stop to learn about the environment.

Mt. Lemmon - beautiful drive.  Snow during winter.

Extra time to kill:

Picacho Peak (hike it if you're in decent shape, the site where the only Civil War battle in Arizona was fought) (closed during summer, 'cause they don't want you to die from heat stroke (my guess)).

San Xavier del Bac Mission (white church painted by 3rd rate artists, skip if you're not into religion.)


In short, if you book through an online company, you will most likely be treated like an ugly red-headed stepchild and be sent to the worst rooms in the hotel.  If you don't have a car, you may be stuck eating in the hotel restaurant.  I heard from others that it was actually pretty good.  I didn't take the chance.  There are a few fast food (Burger King, Subway) joints a few blocks away (5-10 minutes walk).  Free airport shuttle.  I didn't hear any commercial planes, but I heard a few jet fighters flying around.  They were loud, but only during the day and didn't occur often.


I will probably not return.  Didn't like the way I was treated.

text:
My husband and I made reservations at Sidney Street Cafe to celebrate Valentine's Day. We had never been before, but it seems like such a significant "player" in the St. Louis food scene and so well-recommended that it was time to give it a try.

When we arrived at the restaurant, it looked a bit dark at the bar, but as we walked toward the hostess, we saw inside the dining area that it was warmer and brighter. The hostess led us away from that dining area, down a hallway toward another room. I felt like I had left one restaurant and been taken to another that could aptly be named "The Dungeon." The room had skylights (it was after 5:30 in the winter, so no light to speak of there) hanging lights, there was a tiny candle on the table, but it really was just so dim that I felt myself leaning in to see the person across the table from me. We were told it was romantic, but this restaurant's "back room" is on the wrong side of the line between romantic and a creepy cellar.

The hostess set down a wine list and a small board containing a list of appetizers. We wondered what the list of main courses was so we could decide between them and the chef's tasting menu. Our waiter arrived and was not rude, but set the tone of painful pretentiousness for the rest of our visit - every ingredient of every dish was described in minute detail. I think restaurants believe this is part of the "theater of the experience," but it's just too much. That's not to say that the food did not warrant additional explanation, but people cannot process and retain a description of every ingredient that goes into every entree, appetizer, and dessert. After a lengthy description of two of the appetizers (there were about 10 on the board), I tuned the waiter out and just let him finish. At the end, he did mention that the chef's tasting menu was an option and contained five courses, including an amuse-bouche. I think that it is incorrect to advertise an amuse-bouche as a course. Amuse-bouche should be a "gift" from the chef to give them a glimpse of what is to come.

We were given time to consider the options, still without a dinner menu. When the waiter returned, he handed us the dinner menu and asked if we would like to order an appetizer. We should have gotten the dinner menu in advance in order to have time to decide between the listed options and the tasting menu, but we were committed to getting the artisan cheeses and the house-made charcuterie so we did not go the route of the tasting menu. The items were surprisingly scant. There were 16 pieces of meat arranged in rows of 4 on the charcuterie board. Other than the half-rounds of head cheese, the slices were shaved incredibly thinly and were tiny. I would rather have paid a little more to get something of more substance. The flavors of both plates were just ok. Between the two, the best part was the small pretzel rolls that arrived with the charcuterie board, which were chewy, fresh, and flavorful.

Again for the dinner course, we listened to the litany of preparations and ingredients that went into every dish. It was especially difficult to follow for the items that were off the menu. At one point, I heard the waiter talking about taking a blood orange, freezing it, shattering it, and then sprinkling the frozen shards over one of the dishes. That just seems like a lot of work to have something 'different' to tell diners. I did end up ordering the pork belly and my husband ordered the steak Au Poivre. I felt like my pork belly meal was well-prepared and tasty; I would not order it again because for my taste it became too rich, but that is my preference rather than a failing of the restaurant. My husband ordered his steak medium-rare. If a restaurant chooses to give a diner only a portion of a full strip steak and cut it for them, then they should be highly aware of the doneness of the meat they are serving. The steak my husband was served was definitely medium. It was served on top of what was essentially a fried mashed potato cake, which was delectable.

We did not try dessert as we had other plans, which was somewhat relieving to me as I didn't think that I could follow another at-length description. This restaurant has potential, but there is work to be done in finding balance. Preparation and ingredients are important, but if the food is good enough, it can speak for itself without making the diner tired and confused at the ordering stage. Whatever is being done to create a warm atmosphere in the front needs to be transitioned to the uninviting back. The waiter having a loud "look at me" conversation about "the foie I had in LA" needs to take it down a notch. I likely won't go here again; it's worth going once to make up your own mind, but I would strongly encourage you to visit other restaurants in other cities with comparable Zagat ratings before crowning Sidney Street the standard by which all others should be judged.

The review text expresses disappointment with the dining experience, citing issues with the atmosphere, service, and food quality, which aligns with the predicted rating.

Just went to a wedding reception that was catered by Peachtree & Ward at their Radnor reception venue: Pomme.  I was super impressed from beginning to end.

Reception Venue:  It was beautiful and natural.  Even though it was sleeting outside, I could see the gorgeous potential of this site.  To get to the reception area, you cross a bridge over a lake inhabited by real swans (although, word on the street is that they are not very friendly).  The reception area has great natural lighting and beautiful large spherical lamps.  There is also a cocktail hour reception area on the bottom level which opens up to allow for an outdoor heated tent for more cocktail space.  The reception manager for the night was also very helpful as we tried to set up the decorations for the venue before the guests came.  They seemed very flexible and accommodating.

Cocktail Hour:  The food was delicious and the service was amazing!  I have been to many receptions with passed hors d'oeuvres but none with such great variety and service as the reception I went to this past Saturday.  The bites were amazing!  From crispy phyllo dough wrapped crab rolls, mushroom duxelle triangles, tuna tartare on a crispy potato chip (think: kettle-cooked style), peking duck rolls (o-m-g possibly the most delicious invention ever--it was like a crispy Peking Duck wrap you make at an authentic Chinese restaurant), new potato skins with smoked salmon and creme fraiche, and cuban sandwich bites (my least fave of the group but really with such stellar bites, someone has to be the so-to-speak "loser" even if it was also good).  I never felt like I was in want of an hors d'oeuvres and even with a group of famished Asians (trust me, not a group that you want to keep hungry), there were so many servers still with hot and fresh appetizers.  Also, the servers were really attentive...it's like they could read your mind when your face was saying "oh no, I couldn't possibly eat another" but the little piggy inside of you was saying "oh please insist because this is like heaven in a bite!" they would know and make sure to find you.  As if they passed hors d'oeuvres weren't enough, they also had stations with philly cheesesteak sliders (cute, gooey, and cheesey), pretzel bites (with mustard dips), and a nacho chip/juicy pulled pork taco station with mango salsa, guac, and all the typicals.  

Seated Dinner:  Dinner was served in three courses and always very timely.  We started with some mixed greens and a caramelized onion tart (with cheese--my fave!).  Next, was butternut squash ravioli--loved the filling but by this point, I had filled up way too much during cocktail hour so I couldn't finish all of the wrapping.  The main course was a perfectly cooked miso glazed cod over watercress and lime-infused rice.  It was delicious but I was so stuffed from everything else!

Dessert:  Dessert had three options: vanilla and chocolate milkshakes (in shots), adorably cute but possibly too tiny mini coffee & strawberry gelato cones, and little jars filled with shortcake, strawberries, and whipped cream.  The jars were a great idea but I think it would have been even better with vanilla custard at the bottom and whipped cream on top--it needed some other flavor/consistency to bring it all together.  Otherwise, it would have been a rockstar finish.  Best of all, they served FRENCH PRESS coffee with dessert--both decaf and regular.  I mean, if you're gonna serve coffee, at least do it right! :)

Overall, I was super impressed by the service and the quality quality quality of the food!  Really spectacular!

So my friend and I went to this place for a nice get away and tried some good Italian food.  I recently cam back from a trip from Italy so my taste buds still remember the good food I had there but here's what I found about Ca'Dario!

Pros:   Good seafood antipasti
I really liked the seafood mussels and clam soup. A bit salty to my taste but very good flavor.  I used to go to Brophy Brothers right at the pier in Santa Barbara but that place is always overcrowded and this soup at Ca'Dario tastes more fresh.

I ordered Penne alla boscaiola.  Good sauce. I like the pasta more al dente like real Italians do, but I guess most Americans like it more soft so this is somewhere in the middle. If you don't like too al dente, this is perfect for you.

Gnocchi is really fresh and I liked it a lot.  If you are a big gnocchi fan, you should try it out. I like it a bit harder but I could tell it was fresh and flavorful.

The portions are not small so secondi isn't really necessary unless you would like to share with others.  I'd like to come here during dinner time with more people and try different things next time.

Cons:  As I mentioned above, the pasta could be a bit more al dente, but that's totally up to everyone's preference so I'll leave that up to you.  This is not cheap but not too expensive either.  It's Santa Barbara so relative to other places, this is not a surprise.  

I didn't think that there were anything very special or unique though, so ended up going to the seafood market right by the pier and got some fresh white fish and uni (sea urchin) and made my own pasta with it, and that was yummy- you guys should try that too:)

It's really hard for me to give this place a rating. How much you like this place kind of depends on what you're looking for in a bar. If you want a crowded, super fratty bar filled with college students and other 20-something-year-olds and you want to get super wasted, this is THE place to go. However, if you don't like fratstars or crowds or waiting forever to get a drink or being at a bar with people who are still in college or still act like they're in college or waiting in line forever to get into a bar, then you should avoid this place. 

Even though this place is very large with several outdoor bars, a few different rooms, including one with a stage where they have live music some nights, and a some nice outdoor patios, on Thurs/Fri/Sat nights, it still gets completely jam-packed. On Thursday nights, they have $1 Miller Lite drafts and this really brings out the underaged college students. The Thursday night crowd is usually incredibly young, so don't be surprised if you go on a Thursday night and you see some kids who don't even look old enough to drive yet. Also, on their more popular nights (Thurs/Fri/Sat), they charge for valet parking, which tends to get full later in the evening, but on less popular nights they have free valet parking, which is nice. 

On Friday nights, MacDinton's has their happy hour from 6pm-8pm, which is all you can drink for $10. The lines to get into happy hour can get extremely long, and then they give you a teeny tiny cup, which you again have to wait in line for every time you want to get a refill. 

The bouncers here can also be huge pricks sometimes. I've seen people get thrown out for no reason at all, and I've even almost been thrown out myself for no reason. 

If you're 25 or under, make sure you have 2 forms of ID (i.e. driver's license and something else with your name on it, such as a credit card). They can be pretty strict about this and I've had friends who have come and only brought their driver's license and then been turned away. 

I have had some nights where I've had a LOT of fun at MacDinton's but those nights generally involved a ton of alcohol and some fuzzy memories. Being completely sober here can be pretty miserable. Overall, this place can be a lot of fun, given the right circumstances and if you're into the "MacDinton's scene". text:
Has Adobe jumped the shark?

Adobe became one of my regular haunts in South Philly over the past 7 years. Mostly because I love that they have karaoke on both Friday and Saturday. It's entertaining and good, social fun.  However this past Saturday the experience was a complete bust.

We came around 10ish and immediately put in some songs to sing. We waited hours and in the meantime some people sang two or three times, and some that had put in songs after us were going first.  We were informed by a nearby patron, "You have to go complain to the guy, then he'll play your song."  I glance up to see a line 7 or 8 people deep at the DJ area. People had actually queued up to complain so that they could go up and sing. The DJ had a mess of papers everywhere, and others were also complaining because there is no more paper to write songs on.  I simply have never seen this level of disorganization for a karaoke DJ.  It's a shame that the previous DJ Amanda left.  She was amazing at organizing the song flow, being fair and pleasing everyone, letting people know when there were too many songs in and what the wait would be.

Since I'm not getting my karaoke on, I decide to do some more drinking and go to the bar.  But each time we try to get drinks we are usually vaguely ignored for about 20 minutes.  There are piles of credit card receipts and dirty glasses everywhere on the bar.  The bartenders were working, and friendly, but were totally in the weeds and unable to keep up.

So, I decide to play some foosball. The other main reason I love Adobe is their free foosball table in the back dining room. I'm watching four people play, considering asking to jump in on the next game.  Then I realize they have yet to replace the two missing men from the table.  Not only that, now one of the rods is missing a screw and completely pulling out of the table.  These issues would only take a few little screws or replacements parts.

I return to my group of friends in the karaoke room where it's about 90 uncomfortable degrees.  No songs to be sung. No drinks to be had. No foosball to be played. And I realize the horrifying truth that, although Adobe was always a dive where the food was horribly overpriced, it was usually a dive where I could get at least get karaoke, beer, and foosball.  Adobe had moved beyond a fun dive to a dump, where they don't care to hire a competent karaoke DJ (their bread and butter), they don't care to hire another bartender for extremely busy Fridays and Saturdays, and they don't care to buy a few screws to fix the foosball table. I hope the managers read this, because without a bit of extra effort you will start to loose the patrons that supported your business for so long.
llama_8b_pred_reasoning: The review text expresses strong dissatisfaction with the experience at Adobe, citing disorganization, long wait times, and neglect of basic services. All models (BERT, LR, SVM, NB) agree with this assessment, providing a consistent rating of 2 stars.
